sections.overview: The American bison is a large hoofed ruminant native to North America. Before European settlement, it ranged from northern Mexico to interior Alaska. Two forms are commonly distinguished: plains bison in the south and wood bison farther north.
sections.identification: Its massive head, shoulder hump and short hindquarters create a distinctive profile. Both sexes have short, curved horns. Long hair covers the head, shoulders and forelegs, but the rear coat is shorter. Adults shed much of this winter coat in spring. Plains bison usually have a smaller, rounder hump than wood bison. Typical adults are about 2.7–3.8 m long and 1.8–2.0 m high; bulls commonly weigh about 907–998 kg and cows about 454 kg. Bulls are markedly larger, although values vary among subspecies and populations.
sections.habitat: Bison use grasslands, prairies, sedge meadows, shrublands and some woods. Historically, herds moved over immense areas. Today, free-ranging and conservation herds occupy fragments of the former range; fences and management often limit movement.
sections.diet: Bison graze year-round, mainly on grasses and sedges, as well as flowering plants and leaves when available. In winter, they sweep snow aside with the head to uncover plants. They need water daily.
sections.behavior: Herds vary with sex, age and season: females and young commonly group together, while mature bulls may be solitary or form male groups. Bison alternate grazing, resting and rumination. They move as food and water change, wallow in loose soil, and bulls clash during the summer rut.
sections.reproduction: Mating occurs mainly from late June to September. After about 285 days, a female usually gives birth to one calf in spring. The reddish calf soon follows the herd, nurses for seven to eight months and is weaned by its first year. Females may breed at two to three years; males often breed later.
sections.ecology: Grazing, trampling, wallowing and movement disturb prairie plants and soils, creating varied growing conditions. Seeds caught in the coat travel elsewhere, while dung returns nutrients to soil. These effects create a mosaic of plant communities and small habitats, shaped by landscape and herd management.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN Red List assessment, dated 1 September 2016 and published in 2017, classified the species as Near Threatened. It counted wild and conservation herds, not commercial livestock; most American bison are managed for production. The assessment cited few viable populations and many small, isolated herds. It also identified habitat loss and genetic risks, including cattle introgression and hybridization between subspecies.
